question: What is a JWT token and what are its three parts?
title: JWT Token Structure — Header, Payload, Signature Explained
direct_answer: A JWT is a compact, URL-safe format for carrying claims. The common signed compact form has three Base64url parts: a protected header, a claims payload, and a MAC or digital signature that protects integrity. Base64url is encoding, not encryption, so payload claims are readable. Encrypted JWTs use JWE and have a different compact structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JWT structure and purpose — foundational knowledge for implementing any JWT-based authentication system
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing base64 encoding with encryption — the payload is readable by anyone, so sensitive data like passwords should never be stored in it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a JWS signature or MAC protects integrity but not confidentiality, distinguish JWS from JWE, and never paste a real credential into an untrusted decoder

sections.title: Understanding JWT Structure and Purpose
sections.content:
A JWT is a compact, URL-safe format for carrying claims. The familiar three-part value is a **signed JWT represented as a compact JWS**: a protected header, a claims payload, and a signature or MAC. The header names details such as the signing algorithm. The payload contains claims. The last part protects integrity and authenticity when the key and algorithm are validated.

Each part uses Base64url encoding, which is not encryption, so do not put secrets in a readable signed payload. A signature may use an HMAC or a public-key digital-signature algorithm; calling every signature a ‘cryptographic hash’ is incomplete. A JWT can support a stateless bearer-token design, but the application may still check users, permissions, revocation state, or other server data. Encrypted JWTs use JWE and have a different compact structure.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a JWT
sections.content:
blue|Protected header|~xxxxx.|names an accepted algorithm|may include key metadata|Base64url encoded
emerald|Claims payload|~yyyyy.|registered or custom claims|readable in a signed token|never put secrets here
violet|Signature or MAC|~zzzzz|protects header + payload integrity|verified with the correct key|does not encrypt the claims

sections.title: Creating and Parsing a JWT in Spring Boot
When to Use JWT Tokens
sections.content:
Use a signed JWT when several parties need a compact claims token that can be verified with an agreed key and token profile. It is common for OAuth 2.0 access or identity tokens, but JWT is a format rather than a complete login, SSO, revocation, or authorization design.

Choose it only after comparing opaque tokens and sessions. Consider claim freshness, audience separation, key rotation, token size, confidentiality, client storage, revocation, and whether each service should verify tokens itself. Do not share one symmetric secret across many services merely for convenience; asymmetric verification can limit who is able to issue tokens.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting secrets in a signed payload**: Base64url is readable encoding. Keep signed-token claims non-secret and minimal.
- **Validating only the signature**: restrict algorithms and trusted keys and validate the issuer, audience, and time claims required by the token profile.
- **Omitting a bounded lifetime from an access-token policy**: RFC 7519 makes exp optional, but a security profile should deliberately define token lifetime and early-revocation behavior.
- **Calling every JWT a three-part signature**: encrypted JWTs use JWE and can have a five-part compact form.
- **Pasting production tokens into public tools**: a bearer token is a credential; inspect only safe test data locally.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Common signed form**: protected header, claims payload, and signature or MAC, Base64url-encoded and dot-separated
**Base64 vs encryption**: Base64 is encoding for transport, not security — anyone can decode the payload, so never store passwords or API keys
**Validation**: restrict accepted algorithms, use the trusted key, and validate required issuer, audience, and time claims
**Not automatically stateless**: JWT is a token format; the application may still check permissions or revocation data
**Encrypted form**: JWE uses a different compact structure when claim confidentiality is required

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A JWT is a compact format for carrying claims. The common signed compact form has a protected header, a claims payload, and a signature or MAC separated by dots. Base64url only encodes the header and payload, so their contents are readable and must not contain secrets. The last part protects integrity when the receiver restricts the accepted algorithm and verifies it with the trusted key. An API should also validate the issuer, audience, and time claims required by its token profile. JWT can be used in a stateless bearer-token flow, but the format itself does not guarantee statelessness or remove every server-side lookup. Encrypted JWTs use JWE and do not have the same three-part shape.

speakable_v2.hook: The familiar three-part JWT is a compact signed JWS: readable claims plus integrity protection, not encryption.

beats.content: The common signed compact form has three dot-separated parts: a protected header, a claims payload, and a signature or MAC. The algorithm may be asymmetric or symmetric and must be restricted by the receiver's policy.

The receiver verifies the last part with a trusted key, but signature verification alone does not make the token acceptable. It must also validate the issuer, audience, and time claims required by its profile.
Base64url is encoding, not encryption. Anyone holding a signed JWT can usually read its header and claims, so keep secrets out of that payload and treat the whole bearer token as a credential.

An access-token profile commonly requires an exp claim so the token stops being accepted after a bounded time. Expiry is not the only revocation control: key changes, introspection, token-version checks, or a denylist may invalidate a token earlier when the design supports them.

speakable_v2.cap: A compact signed JWT carries readable claims and integrity protection. Trust it only after full algorithm, key, issuer, audience, and time validation.
followup_handoff: The specific claims to include — sub, iat, exp, iss — is a natural follow-up question.
We can also cover the difference between HS256 symmetric signing and RS256 asymmetric signing.

question: What are JWT claims and what standard claims should you include?
title: JWT Claims — Standard and Custom Claims Explained
direct_answer: JWT claims are name-value pairs about the token or subject. Registered names include iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, and jti. RFC 7519 makes them optional; an application profile decides which are required. For an access token, requiring and validating expiry, issuer, and audience is a common security policy. Custom claims should be small and should not contain secrets.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical JWT implementation knowledge — understanding claims shows you've actually built JWT auth, not just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the JWT specification requires exp, or validating only the signature while ignoring the token profile's issuer, audience, time, and revocation rules
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between registered claims (standardized), public claims (collision-resistant), and private claims (custom for your app), and explain security implications of each claim type

sections.title: Understanding JWT Claims and Their Types
sections.content:
Claims are name-value pairs in a JWT payload. **Registered claims** such as iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, and jti have meanings defined by RFC 7519. **Public claims** use collision-resistant names, often registered with IANA, while **private claims** are agreed between the producer and consumer.

RFC 7519 does not require every registered claim. The token profile for an application decides which claims are mandatory. For an access token, a common policy requires a short expiry and validates issuer and audience, but the exact lifetime comes from the risk and workflow. Expiry is not the only possible revocation control: systems can use short-lived tokens, key rotation, token version checks, introspection, or a denylist, each with its own cost. Claims in a signed JWT are readable, so keep them minimal and never store secrets.

sections.title: Claim Types and Key Claims
sections.content:
blue|Registered|~RFC-defined names|iss / sub / aud|exp / nbf / iat / jti|optional unless a profile requires them
emerald|Public|~collision-resistant name|may use the IANA registry|shared across systems|document its meaning
violet|Private|~producer and consumer agree|roles or tenant id|not globally standardized|keep payload small
rose|Validation policy|~profile-specific|required issuer + audience|bounded lifetime|optional revocation checks

sections.title: Building JWT with Standard and Custom Claims
When to Use Different Claim Types
sections.content:
Define a token profile first. It may require sub for the subject, iss for the trusted issuer, aud for the intended service, and exp to bound the lifetime. Add nbf only when the token must not work before a time, and jti when a token identifier serves a real purpose.

Private claims can carry small authorization facts such as a tenant or scope, but avoid volatile or sensitive profile data. There is no universal one-kilobyte rule; smaller tokens reduce request overhead and reduce the amount of readable data exposed. Consumers must validate the claims required by the profile rather than accepting every correctly signed token.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing specification with policy**: RFC 7519 makes registered claims optional, while an access-token profile should normally require a bounded lifetime and other context checks.
- **Using a fixed lifetime rule**: token lifetime depends on risk, refresh design, client, and revocation controls; 15 minutes to 24 hours is not a universal safe range.
- **Putting secrets in claims**: a signed payload is Base64url encoded, not encrypted.
- **Checking only the signature**: also validate the accepted algorithm, trusted key, issuer, audience, and applicable time claims.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **sub (subject)**: The user or entity the token represents — typically the user ID from your database, used for authorization decisions
**exp (expiration)**: NumericDate after which the token must not be accepted; optional in RFC 7519 but commonly required by access-token profiles
**iat (issued at)**: Unix timestamp when token was created — useful for token age validation and security auditing
**iss (issuer)**: Identifies who created the token — prevents token confusion when multiple services issue tokens
**aud (audience)**: Identifies intended recipients — services should reject tokens where they're not in the audience list

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: JWT claims are name-value pairs in the payload. Registered names such as issuer, subject, audience, expiration, not-before, issued-at, and JWT ID have meanings defined by RFC 7519. Public claims use collision-resistant names, while private claims are agreed between the producer and consumer. The RFC does not require every registered claim; the application's token profile does. An access-token profile commonly requires a bounded expiry and validates issuer and audience. Keep custom claims small and avoid secrets because a signed payload is readable. Signature validation alone is not enough, and expiry is not the only possible revocation control: short lifetimes, key changes, introspection, token-version checks, or denylists can be used when their trade-offs fit.

content: sub — Subject, typically the user ID or username
iat — Issued At, Unix timestamp of when the token was created

beats.content: Keep the payload small because a bearer JWT is commonly sent with each protected request. Include only stable facts the receiving service actually needs, and remember that signed claims are readable rather than secret.

A shorter access-token lifetime limits how long a stolen token can be used, while a refresh-token design can renew access without a full login. The actual lifetime and whether refresh tokens are appropriate depend on the client, risk, and revocation design.

question: What library do you use to work with JWT in Spring Boot?
title: JWT Libraries in Spring Boot — JJWT and Spring Security OAuth2
direct_answer: For a Spring Security resource server, prefer spring-security-oauth2-resource-server with the JOSE support used for JWT decoding and validation. JJWT is another library when the application itself needs lower-level token creation or parsing. There is no single required library; choose maintained support that validates the expected algorithms, issuer, audience, timestamps, and keys.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical library knowledge and awareness of the JWT ecosystem in Java — shows you've implemented JWT, not just studied it theoretically
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing a library exists and trying to manually parse JWT with Base64 decoding and JSON parsing, which is error-prone and insecure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish a protected API that can use Spring Security Resource Server from an application that needs lower-level token creation or parsing, and verify the selected library version's dependencies and API

sections.title: JWT Library Roles: Resource Server and JJWT
sections.content:
There is no single JWT library required by Spring Boot. For an API that accepts bearer access tokens, Spring Security's **OAuth 2.0 Resource Server** support is usually the first choice because it connects JWT decoding, validation, authentication, and authorization to the security filter chain. It can validate tokens from an external provider or from an issuer your organization controls.

**JJWT** is a separate library with APIs for creating, signing, parsing, and validating JWTs. A typical JJWT setup uses its API plus a runtime implementation and a JSON module, but the exact artifacts and methods depend on the version and serializer. Choose the library from the application's role, maintained integration, algorithm support, key management, and token profile. Never treat Base64 decoding as validation.

sections.title: Which JWT Library?
sections.content:
blue|Spring Resource Server|~security integration|bearer-token filter + decoder|issuer or trusted keys|first choice for protected APIs
emerald|JJWT|~lower-level JWT library|create or parse tokens|artifact set depends on version|application owns integration
amber|Decision rule|~role + maintenance|issuer versus resource API|algorithm and key support|never validate by Base64 decoding

sections.title: Creating a JWT with Injected Policy
When to Use Each Library
sections.content:
Use Spring Security Resource Server when a Spring API accepts bearer access tokens and needs those tokens converted into Authentication and authorities. The issuer may be external or operated by your own organization; external versus internal is not the deciding line.

Use JJWT when the application needs its lower-level builder or parser APIs and is prepared to own the surrounding key, validation, error, and Spring integration. An authorization server should normally use a maintained authorization-server product or framework instead of inventing an authentication protocol around a token library. Check current documentation for dependency coordinates and APIs because both libraries evolve.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Copying dependency advice across versions**: JJWT's API, runtime implementation, and JSON integration must match; check that version's official installation guide.
- **Decoding without validation**: splitting and Base64-decoding a token proves nothing about its signature, issuer, audience, or lifetime.
- **Hardcoding a signing key**: load keys from an approved secret or key-management system and plan rotation.
- **Accepting the token's algorithm blindly**: configure an allow-list and trusted key source rather than trusting header input.
- **Building custom security unnecessarily**: prefer Resource Server support when it already implements the bearer-token flow.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **No mandated library**: Spring Boot applications can choose maintained JWT and OAuth support that fits their role
**JJWT modules**: a typical setup uses API, runtime implementation, and one JSON integration; verify the selected version
**Fluent API**: Builder pattern for token creation and parser for validation with automatic signature checking
**spring-security-oauth2-resource-server**: Spring's built-in JWT support for OAuth2/OIDC integration
**Selection**: compare issuer or resource-server role, Spring integration, key handling, algorithms, and maintenance

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring Boot does not require one JWT library. For an API that receives bearer access tokens, I would normally start with Spring Security's OAuth 2.0 Resource Server support. It connects token decoding and validation to the security filter chain and can trust an external issuer or keys managed by my own organization. JJWT is a separate lower-level library for building, signing, parsing, and validating JWTs when the application needs that API directly. A common JJWT setup has an API artifact, a runtime implementation, and a JSON integration, but I check the documentation for the chosen version instead of copying dependency or method names from an older example. Whichever option I use, Base64 decoding is not validation: the application still needs an allowed algorithm, trusted key, issuer and audience checks, applicable time checks, and safe key rotation.

question: How does JWT-based authentication work in Spring Boot?
title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot — Request Lifecycle
direct_answer: In a common bearer-token flow, an authorization service issues a signed access token after authentication. The client sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header. Spring Security's resource-server support—or a carefully written custom filter—validates the token's algorithm, signature, issuer, audience, and time claims, converts claims to authorities, and places the resulting Authentication in the SecurityContext for that request.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of end-to-end JWT authentication flow and how it integrates with Spring Security's filter chain
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how the JWT gets from client to server (Authorization header) or how Spring Security's SecurityContext gets populated from the token
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate token issuance from resource-server validation, name BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter and JwtDecoder, and explain that a custom OncePerRequestFilter is not the default solution

sections.title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot
sections.content:
In a common bearer-token flow, an authorization service authenticates the user and issues a signed access token. The client sends it on later requests as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The resource API validates the accepted algorithm, signature, trusted issuer, intended audience, and required time claims before treating the claims as an authenticated principal.

Spring Security can do this through OAuth 2.0 Resource Server support, which supplies the bearer-token filter and JWT decoder. A custom OncePerRequestFilter is an alternative only when the protocol or token format truly needs custom behavior; then the application owns all validation and error handling. After successful validation, Spring stores an Authentication in the SecurityContext for the request and applies request or method authorization. Token storage and CSRF handling remain separate client-design decisions.

sections.title: JWT Login and Request Flows
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Authorization service
authenticates client or user] --> B[Issue signed access token] B --> C[Client sends
Authorization: Bearer token] C --> D[BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter] D --> E[JwtDecoder validates
algorithm, key and required claims] E -->|valid| F[Convert claims to Authentication] E -->|invalid| G[AuthenticationEntryPoint
returns configured 401 response] F --> H[Authorization rules] H -->|allowed| I[Controller] H -->|denied| J[Configured access-denied response] ```

sections.title: JWT Authentication Filter Implementation
When to Use JWT Authentication
sections.content:
Use JWT bearer access tokens when the authorization architecture defines an issuer, intended audiences, trusted keys, required claims, and token lifecycle. Resource Server is a good fit for a Spring API that consumes such tokens.

JWT avoids an HTTP-session lookup, but it does not remove all server state or automatically fit every microservice, SPA, mobile app, or public API. Services may still consult permissions or revocation data. Compare opaque token introspection and sessions, and avoid putting unrelated client and user identities into one token unless the token profile clearly defines their meaning.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing a custom JWT filter first**: Resource Server already handles standard bearer extraction, decoding, Authentication creation, failures, and filter placement.
- **Checking only signature and exp**: also restrict algorithms and trusted keys and validate issuer, audience, and every claim required by the token profile.
- **Building an Authentication from unverified claims**: decode and fully validate before granting authorities.
- **Returning 500 for an invalid token**: use the configured AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler for stable security responses.
- **Calling stateless 'no server state'**: the API may still query users, permissions, token versions, or revocation data.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Login flow**: POST credentials to /login endpoint, server validates against database, generates JWT with user claims, returns token to client
**Authorization header**: Client sends token in every request as Authorization: Bearer <token> — this is the standard way to transmit tokens
**Spring support**: OAuth 2.0 Resource Server can extract and validate bearer JWTs without a hand-written filter
**Validation**: restrict algorithms and verify signature, issuer, audience, and required time claims
**SecurityContext population**: Resource Server creates a protocol-appropriate Authentication after validation and makes it available for the request

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A common JWT bearer flow starts when an authorization service authenticates a user and issues a signed access token. The client sends that token in the Authorization header. The API must validate the accepted algorithm, signature, issuer, audience, and required time claims. In Spring Security, OAuth 2.0 Resource Server support can perform this work and create an Authentication in the SecurityContext, after which URL and method rules authorize the request. A custom OncePerRequestFilter is possible, but it is not required and makes the application responsible for every validation and error case. A stateless HTTP-session policy means the request does not rely on a saved SecurityContext; it does not mean the application can never consult current permissions or revocation data.

speakable_v2.hook: JWT issuance and API validation are separate responsibilities: an authorization service issues a token, and a resource server validates it for each protected request.

beats.content: An authorization service authenticates the client or user according to its protocol and issues a signed access token for a defined audience. The resource API should not invent issuance merely because it consumes JWTs.

The client sends the access token in the Authorization: Bearer header. Spring Security Resource Server uses BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter and a JwtDecoder to validate it and create an Authentication for the request.

A stateless SecurityContext policy means the API does not rely on an HTTP session for later requests. Filter placement is already provided by Resource Server; there is no universal rule to put a custom JWT filter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.
For a protected stateless request, the bearer token is validated again and a request-scoped Authentication is created. Other user, permission, or revocation lookups may still occur.

speakable_v2.cap: The issuer creates a scoped token; the resource server validates the bearer token and required claims before authorizing each request.

question: Where should you store JWT tokens on the client side?
title: JWT Storage — localStorage vs HttpOnly Cookie Security Trade-offs
direct_answer: Token storage depends on the client and threat model. JavaScript-readable storage can let XSS steal a bearer token. An HttpOnly, Secure cookie prevents JavaScript from reading it, but the browser sends it automatically, so the application must address CSRF with SameSite settings and, where needed, a CSRF token. No storage choice replaces XSS prevention, short token lifetime, and careful refresh-token handling.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security awareness and understanding of client-side attack vectors — essential for any full-stack or backend role dealing with authentication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Declaring localStorage or HttpOnly cookies universally safe, or treating SameSite and Content Security Policy as complete substitutes for XSS and CSRF prevention
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose storage from the actual client and origin model, explain what HttpOnly does and does not protect, and cover CSRF, XSS, refresh, logout, and recovery together

sections.title: Client-Side JWT Storage Options and Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Browser token storage is a threat-model decision. A bearer token in localStorage is readable by JavaScript, so an XSS payload can copy and reuse it. A cookie marked HttpOnly cannot be read through document.cookie, which reduces token theft, but the browser sends that cookie automatically on matching requests. That creates a CSRF concern for state-changing requests.

Secure and Path/Domain settings limit transport and scope. SameSite reduces many cross-site cookie sends, but its mode must fit navigation and identity flows and it is not a replacement for every CSRF control. Some applications use a CSRF token as well. HttpOnly also does not make XSS harmless: malicious script can still act as the user through the page. Prefer short-lived access credentials, careful refresh-token handling, XSS prevention, and the storage pattern supported by the client.

sections.title: Two Storage Options, Two Risks
sections.content:
rose|JavaScript-readable storage|~easy Authorization header|XSS can copy bearer token|CSP reduces some risk|still prevent injection
emerald|HttpOnly cookie|~JavaScript cannot read it|browser sends it automatically|reduces token theft|address CSRF explicitly
blue|Whole design|~no universal winner|Secure + narrow cookie scope|bounded access lifetime|safe refresh and logout policy

Cookie value is hidden, but script may act as the user
Browser auto-sends a matching cookie; add suitable controls
Manual — add Authorization header in code
JavaScript and CORS rules control the target
Domain, Path, SameSite, credentials mode, and CORS all matter
Do not copy browser storage advice
Use platform-protected credential storage where available

sections.title: Storing in localStorage (XSS-exposed)
Storing in an HttpOnly Cookie (reduces token readability)
Choosing the Right Storage Strategy
sections.content:
Choose storage from the client and attack model. A native mobile app should use its platform's protected credential storage rather than a browser rule. In a browser, keeping an access token only in memory can limit persistent theft but changes refresh and navigation behavior. JavaScript-readable persistent storage is convenient for an Authorization header but exposes the bearer token to XSS.

An HttpOnly, Secure cookie reduces JavaScript token theft. Its SameSite, Domain, Path, lifetime, and CSRF controls must match the deployment, especially for cross-site login or API calls. There is no one maximum-security recipe for every app. Keep credentials short-lived enough for the risk, rotate refresh tokens when the design uses them, prevent XSS, and test login, refresh, logout, CSRF, and cross-site flows.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling CSP a fix for readable tokens**: Content Security Policy is useful defense in depth but does not make all XSS impossible.
- **Calling HttpOnly XSS-proof**: it hides the cookie value from document.cookie, while injected script may still perform authenticated actions.
- **Using SameSite mechanically**: Strict, Lax, and None change legitimate navigation and identity flows; SameSite=None also requires Secure in modern browsers.
- **Ignoring CSRF because the cookie holds a JWT**: risk follows automatic cookie sending, not the token format.
- **Copying browser advice to native apps**: use the platform's protected credential storage and lifecycle APIs.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **XSS**: injected JavaScript can copy a bearer token from JavaScript-readable storage and can still act through the page when a cookie is HttpOnly
**CSRF**: forged requests matter when the browser automatically sends authentication; SameSite reduces risk but may not be the only control
**HttpOnly flag**: Server-side cookie attribute that prevents JavaScript access — set in Set-Cookie header, not accessible via document.cookie
**SameSite=Strict**: sharply limits cross-site cookie sending but must fit legitimate navigation and identity flows
**SameSite=Lax**: Cookie sent on same-site requests and top-level GET navigations — balances security with usability for links and redirects

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: In a browser, JavaScript-readable storage makes it easy to add a bearer token to the Authorization header, but an XSS payload can copy that token. An HttpOnly cookie prevents document.cookie from reading the value, which reduces theft, but the browser sends the cookie automatically and the application must address CSRF. SameSite helps but must fit the real navigation and sign-in flow, and it is not the only control in every deployment. HttpOnly does not make XSS harmless because injected script can still act through the page. There is no universal winner: choose the design from the client, origin layout, refresh and logout behavior, XSS and CSRF threats, and recovery needs. Keep cookie scope narrow, use HTTPS, bound token lifetimes, and test the complete credential lifecycle.

speakable_v2.hook: Browser token storage is a threat-model choice: JavaScript-readable storage exposes token theft, while cookies introduce automatic sending and CSRF decisions.

beats.content: JavaScript-readable storage makes it easy to attach a bearer token to an Authorization header, but injected script in that origin can copy and replay the token. Content Security Policy can reduce some risk but is not a complete XSS cure.

An HttpOnly cookie prevents document.cookie from reading its value, which reduces token theft. It does not stop injected script from acting through the page. Because the browser automatically sends matching cookies, design CSRF protection using suitable SameSite, CSRF-token, origin, and cookie-scope controls.

beats.content: There is no universal winner. Choose from the client type, origin layout, XSS and CSRF exposure, refresh and logout behavior, and recovery requirements. HttpOnly, Secure, and narrow cookie scope help but do not eliminate XSS or replace CSRF analysis.

speakable_v2.cap: No storage option is risk-free; test the complete token, cookie, CSRF, XSS, refresh, and logout lifecycle for the real client.
followup_handoff: Content Security Policy is a browser-level defense that reduces XSS risk when using localStorage.

question: What is the difference between stateful and stateless authentication?
title: Stateful vs Stateless Authentication — Session vs JWT
direct_answer: Stateful authentication stores server-side session state and usually identifies it with a session cookie. In a stateless request flow, each request carries enough credential information to authenticate without an HTTP session; a JWT bearer token is one option, not the definition. A JWT need not contain all user data, and early revocation is possible through short lifetimes, key changes, introspection, or a denylist—each adds a trade-off or server-side state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architectural understanding of authentication approaches and how they impact system scalability and session management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Equating stateless with JWT, saying sessions cannot scale, or saying a signed JWT can never be rejected before expiry
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare HTTP-session dependence, shared stores, credential size and exposure, permission freshness, and several revocation choices without using a fixed lifetime recipe

sections.title: Two Fundamentally Different Approaches to Authentication
sections.content:
The difference is whether one request depends on authentication state saved from an earlier request. In a **stateful session**, the server stores a SecurityContext or related session data and the client sends an identifier, usually a cookie. In a **stateless request flow**, each request brings a credential that can be authenticated without reading an HTTP session.

A JWT bearer token is one stateless option, but stateless does not mean that every user detail must be inside the token or that the application can never query a database. It may still load current permissions, check a token version, or consult a revocation list. Likewise, sessions can scale through a shared store without sticky routing. The useful comparison is session dependence, credential size, revocation design, client behavior, and operational cost.

emerald|Stateless request|~credential on every request|JWT, opaque token, or Basic|no HTTP-session dependency|may still consult server data
amber|Token lifecycle|~design explicitly|bounded access-token lifetime|refresh and key policy|optional denylist or introspection

sections.title: Stateful Session Configuration
Stateless JWT Configuration
When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **sessions** when server-controlled login state, browser cookies, and direct central invalidation fit the application. Sessions can scale with a shared store; sticky routing is one alternative, not a requirement.

Use a **stateless request credential** when each request should authenticate without an HTTP-session lookup. A JWT is one option, while an opaque bearer token with introspection or HTTP Basic may also be stateless at that layer. JWTs are not required for microservices, mobile apps, SPAs, or cross-origin use. Define bounded access-token lifetime and refresh or early-revocation behavior from the client, threat model, issuer, and recovery needs rather than copying a fixed duration.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Claiming JWT is always better**: sessions and tokens solve different client, lifecycle, and operating needs.
- **Saying a signed JWT can never be revoked**: early rejection is possible through introspection, a token version, denylist, or key policy, but those choices add state or operational cost.
- **Saying sessions cannot scale**: a shared session store is a normal scale-out design.
- **Putting a full profile in the token**: keep claims small, stable, non-secret, and limited to the consuming service's contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Stateful**: Server stores session data, client sends session ID cookie, server looks up data on each request
**Stateless request**: authentication does not depend on an HTTP session; JWT is only one credential format
**Scaling**: sessions can use a shared store; stateless requests avoid that particular shared state
**Revocation**: sessions are easy to invalidate centrally; tokens need an explicit lifetime and revocation policy
**No universal lifetime**: choose access and refresh lifetimes from risk, client, and recovery needs

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Stateful authentication saves session state on the server and gives the client an identifier, usually a cookie. A later request depends on that stored session. In a stateless request flow, every request carries a credential that can be authenticated without the HTTP session. A JWT bearer token is one option, but it does not need to contain every user detail, and the application may still query current permissions or revocation state. For example, a browser can send `JSESSIONID` while two application instances read the same server-side session; a mobile client can instead send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and each instance validates that token. Sessions are straightforward to invalidate centrally. Token systems need an explicit policy using bounded lifetimes and, when required, introspection, token versions, denylists, or key changes. The choice depends on the client, revocation requirement, credential exposure, and operating model rather than a rule that one scales and the other does not.

seo.metaTitle: Stateful vs Stateless Authentication — Session vs JWT | Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn stateful vs stateless authentication — server-side sessions vs JWT, horizontal scaling advantage, JWT invalidation problem, Spring Security STATELESS.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: Stateful and stateless describe whether a request depends on saved HTTP-session authentication; JWT is only one possible stateless credential.

beats.content: Stateful authentication stores session data on the server. A later request carries a session identifier and depends on that saved state. Central invalidation is direct, although distributed propagation and already-running requests still need consideration.

Multiple instances can use sticky routing or a shared session store. A shared store adds an operational dependency, but sessions are a normal scale-out design rather than an automatic scaling failure.

A self-contained JWT can be validated without an HTTP-session lookup when the instance has trusted keys and validation policy. The application may still query permissions, users, token versions, or a denylist, so it is inaccurate to say the server stores nothing.

Early rejection is possible through introspection, a token version, a denylist, account checks, or key changes, each with cost and scope. Choose access lifetime and refresh-token rotation or revocation from the actual risk rather than a universal number.

speakable_v2.cap: Sessions and stateless credentials move state and lifecycle costs to different places; choose using the client, revocation, freshness, exposure, and operating model.
followup_handoff: Refresh token rotation is how most production systems handle the JWT revocation problem.
Spring Security's SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS is how you tell Spring not to create sessions for JWT-based APIs.
